title: Matching a Honey Bottle to an Existing Cap
imageCaption: Bottle and cap options we prepared during the customer’s sourcing discussion.
summary: A customer came to us with caps they had already purchased locally. We helped them find a compatible honey bottle and compare a bottle-only order with a complete bottle-and-cap supply plan, including delivered cost.
displayStatus: Bottle, cap and delivery plan agreed
facts: Existing lid versus a complete new pack
Bottle, cap and delivered-cost plan completed
sections: What the Customer Asked Us For

The customer had already purchased caps from a local supplier and needed a compatible plastic honey bottle. They also wanted us to recommend the right bottle capacity for the intended honey weight and calculate the delivered cost.
Choosing the Right Bottle Capacity

We started with the target honey net weight rather than choosing a bottle by its milliliter rating alone. Because honey and water do not weigh the same, this helped us shortlist a bottle with enough working capacity and headspace for the customer’s actual fill.
Making Sure the Existing Cap Would Fit

We asked the customer for the full cap specification because two caps that look alike may not have the same thread or seal. We then offered two practical routes: send bottle samples to test with the customer’s cap, or quote a complete bottle-and-cap assembly from us, including a dispensing-valve option.
Comparing the Supply Options

We priced the bottle, matching closure and delivery arrangement separately, then compared local consolidation with direct delivery. This let the customer compare the full landed supply plan instead of looking only at the bottle unit price.
The Plan We Agreed with the Customer

By the end of the project, we had agreed on the bottle route, the steps for checking cap compatibility and a complete delivered-cost comparison. The customer knew which components, fit checks and delivery costs were included before placing the order.
What Helped Us Move the Project Forward

The customer shared the target honey weight, existing-cap information, order quantity and destination with us. With those details, we could compare the bottle-only route and the matched complete pack side by side, keeping cap fit and delivered cost in the same decision.

title: Selecting 250 ml and 320 ml Honey Bear Bottles
imageCaption: The 250 ml and 320 ml bear bottle formats we compared for one customer project.
summary: A customer wanted two honey pack sizes with the same familiar bear-bottle look. We helped them build the range around our 250 ml and 320 ml PET bottles, with a clear fill, closure and label plan for each size.
sections: Planning a Two-Size Bear Bottle Range

The customer wanted two related honey pack sizes with the familiar bear-bottle appearance across both. We recommended our 250 ml and 320 ml PET bear bottles and compared their capacities, proportions and shelf presentation together.
Confirming Capacity and Honey Fill

We gave the customer both the catalog capacities and the reference honey fills: approximately 350 g for the 250 ml bottle and 450 g for the 320 ml bottle. The final net weight and headspace would still be approved with the customer’s own honey and chosen fill level.
Sizing the Artwork for Each Bottle

Both bottles keep the molded bear visible around the front panel, but the usable label areas are different. We therefore recommended a separate actual-size artwork proof for each bottle instead of simply shrinking one label file and assuming it would sit correctly on both curved bodies.
Using a Consistent Closure

Both bottles use a 38-400 neck finish, giving the range a practical route to the same closure appearance. Even with the shared neck-finish reference, we would still check each bottle, cap, liner and seal together before approval.
The Final Two-Size Pack

We prepared two defined bottle formats with reference fill weights and a consistent closure direction. Each bottle also had its own label-panel requirements, so the two packs could look related without forcing the same artwork size onto different bodies.
What We Prepared for the Customer
The customer left the project with a coordinated 250 ml and 320 ml bear-bottle range, clear reference fills, a shared neck-finish direction and a separate label specification for each bottle.

title: Preparing a 25 ml Glass Honey Jar for Export
imageCaption: The 25 ml round glass jar and metal lid we selected for the project.
summary: A customer needed a small glass jar for a honey portion pack. We brought the 25 ml jar, matching metal lid, label area and protective export packing together in one order specification.
displayStatus: Jar, lid and export packing agreed
sections: Choosing the 25 ml Jar

The customer needed a compact glass container for a small honey portion. We recommended our 25 ml round jar and paired it with the available metal lid so we could work on the jar and closure as one complete pack.
Confirming the Jar Dimensions

For the packing layout, we used the assembled reference dimensions: 40.5 mm overall height with the lid and a 40 mm body diameter. These dimensions gave us the space needed around each jar for dividers and protective material.
Making the Small Label Area Work

Because the jar body has limited space, we planned the front label at actual size rather than scaling down artwork from a larger jar. If the customer needed more visible brand information, the lid could also carry a separate sticker.
Pairing the Jar with Its Metal Lid
We paired the jar with its metal lid and set out the liner, seal and filling-temperature checks for the assembled sample. This kept the closure choice tied to the customer’s real filling process.
Protecting the Jars for Export

Our standard packing reference was 280 jars per carton. Because the jars are glass, we also planned for dividers and protective materials instead of calculating freight from the jar count alone. We would confirm the final carton dimensions and pallet requirements with the approved packing method.
The Final Packing Specification
We brought the 25 ml jar, matching metal lid, assembled dimensions, label approach, carton count and glass protection together in one export packing specification for the customer.
